strengths: Significance: Opportunistically using spare online-serving capacity for offline inference addresses an important resource-efficiency problem. Sharing model weights and adapting offline work to online demand is a useful systems contribution.

Originality: The combination of layer-level preemption, incremental KV-cache checkpointing, background prefetching, and SLO-aware batching is technically motivated. Exploiting immutable historical KV states to reduce eviction-time blocking is a particularly useful insight, even though preemption and workload colocation have substantial precedent.

Soundness: The implementation and experiments provide evidence that this combination can improve the latency–throughput tradeoff in the tested setting. The evaluation includes a real arrival trace, synthetic burstiness and load sweeps, and component ablations; Section 6.4 shows checkpointing and prefetching recovering throughput lost to latency-aware scheduling.

Presentation: The architecture and checkpoint/resume alternatives are generally explained clearly, especially Figures 3–4. The manuscript identifies concrete implementation choices, including the vLLM version, CUDA streams, memory mappings, and preemption instrumentation.
weaknesses: Soundness—headline results are inconsistent with the reported measurements. Section 6.2 reports 3702 tokens/s for ConServe and 1999 tokens/s for Online-Only, implying approximately 1.85× throughput, not the repeatedly claimed 2.35×. Figure 5 calls 86% an offline-throughput ratio, although 3702/4308 compares the reported overall throughputs. Section 6.4.1 also reports a reduction from 1346 ms to 446 ms as 71.4%, whereas it is approximately 66.9%; the corresponding Figure 8 bar appears closer to 340 ms. These discrepancies require reconciliation before the quantitative claims can be trusted.

Soundness and reproducibility—the central scheduling pseudocode contains consequential errors. Algorithm 2, lines 10–11, exits when predicted latency exceeds the TTFT objective, precisely when the prose says preemption should occur; the break is also outside a loop. Algorithm 1, line 31, subtracts tokens from the remaining budget when removing an offline request, rather than restoring budget. These could be transcription errors, but the manuscript does not establish which policy produced the results.

Evaluation—the comparisons do not adequately isolate the advantage over competitive alternatives. Online-Only is a useful latency reference but performs no offline work, so higher total throughput alone is not a strong comparative result. The 84× latency improvement is against the authors' vLLM++ extension, whose scheduling and tuning are insufficiently specified. A carefully tuned priority scheduler with chunked prefill and bounded batch sizes, evaluated across its latency–throughput frontier, is needed. The paper also provides no comparison with contemporary serving implementations beyond its vLLM 0.4.2 foundation.

Soundness—the strong performance-isolation claims exceed the evidence. Section 4.5 acknowledges that latency depends on context lengths, but does not specify sufficiently how the profiler models mixed batches, prediction error, queueing delays, or remaining TTFT budgets across chunks. There is no profiler-accuracy evaluation or systematic SLO-tightness sweep. Figure 7 shows TTFT rising to many seconds under heavier or burstier loads, so the accompanying assertion that ConServe consistently avoids SLO violations needs qualification. Matching an overloaded Online-Only baseline is different from satisfying an SLO.

Scope and limitations—all experiments use Llama-2-7B on one A100-40GB. This is useful initial evidence, but does not validate multi-GPU synchronization, pipeline parallelism, different KV-cache architectures, or the long-context and multiple-model compatibility claims in Section 7. The concern is the mismatch between demonstrated scope and broad claims, rather than the existence of these limitations.

Reproducibility—important experimental details are missing: the exact trace segment and sampling seed, LongBench subsets and length handling, offline queue provisioning, batch/chunk limits, profiler construction, percentile aggregation windows, and repeated-run variability. No code or artifact link is supplied. Section 6.1 also says all experiments use tensor parallelism while listing only one GPU. These omissions make the tail-latency results and baseline behavior difficult to reproduce.

Presentation and research ethics: Several plots label the proposed system 'Concerto' rather than ConServe, adding ambiguity alongside the numerical inconsistencies. No material ethical violation is evident from the described systems work and public datasets, but the manuscript provides little discussion of trace privacy or data handling. Overall, the useful design is outweighed by unresolved evidential and reproducibility weaknesses.

strengths: Significance: Harvesting spare online-serving capacity for latency-insensitive inference is a useful practical problem. The distinction between online latency objectives and offline throughput is well motivated by the bursty workload trace.

Originality: The combination of layer-boundary preemption, incremental KV-cache checkpointing, asynchronous restoration, and SLO-aware batching constitutes a coherent systems contribution. Exploiting immutable historical KV states to reduce urgent eviction costs is particularly well matched to autoregressive inference.

Soundness: The implementation and evaluation provide encouraging evidence within the tested configuration. Experiments include a real arrival trace, synthetic ON/OFF transitions, burstiness and request-rate sweeps, and component ablations. Figure 8 supports the usefulness of checkpointing and prefetching beyond scheduling alone.

Presentation: The architectural overview and Figure 4 explain the mechanisms and their intended tradeoffs clearly. Hardware, numerical precision, and the underlying vLLM version are disclosed. I see no material research-ethics concern in the described work.
weaknesses: Soundness—central numerical claims are inconsistent with the reported results. Section 6.2 reports 3702 tokens/s for ConServe versus 1999 for Online-Only, which implies approximately 1.85× throughput, not the repeatedly claimed 2.35×. Figure 5's caption describes 86% of ideal offline throughput, although the plotted metric and the ratio 3702/4308 concern overall throughput. Additionally, Section 6.3.2 reports a minimum vLLM++ TTFT of 4980 ms, whereas the purportedly matching CV=1, 2 requests/s ablation reports 1346 ms. These discrepancies need reconciliation before the headline improvements can be trusted.

Soundness—the supplied scheduling algorithms contradict the intended behavior. Algorithm 2, lines 10–11, exits when predicted latency exceeds the TTFT objective, precisely when the prose says preemption is required; the break is also outside a loop. Algorithm 1 defines a remaining token budget but subtracts tokens when removing a request at line 31, rather than restoring capacity. These may be transcription errors, but they affect the central algorithm and make faithful implementation unreliable.

Soundness—SLO preservation is asserted more strongly than established. Section 4.5 largely budgets individual iterations using offline profiles, without specifying how accumulated queuing time, multi-chunk prefill, context-length variation, or prediction error enter the decision. No profiler accuracy or safety-margin evaluation is provided. Figure 7 shows online TTFT rising substantially with load and burstiness, so proximity to Online-Only cannot establish the accompanying claim that latency-SLO violations are consistently avoided. The paper should distinguish relative isolation from absolute SLO attainment and report violation rates.

Evaluation—the comparison does not convincingly establish superiority over strong serving alternatives. The main competitors are online-only vLLM and an author-built priority extension that aggressively batches offline work. Online-Only usefully measures interference, but its zero offline throughput makes it an incomplete efficiency comparator. Although the SLO-aware ablation is helpful, the paper needs a comparably tuned alternative, such as priority scheduling with bounded chunks and batch sizes, and latency–throughput tradeoff curves under matched SLOs. The 84× improvement over the constructed baseline should not be generalized to existing co-serving systems broadly.

Significance and scope—the evidence covers only Llama-2-7B on one A100-40GB GPU. This supports a specialized proof of concept, but not the broader claims concerning multi-GPU synchronization, tensor/pipeline parallelism, long contexts, or multiple models. Section 7's proposed extensions are reasonable future directions; the concern is that stronger compatibility and generality statements remain unvalidated. In particular, distributed preemption overhead cannot be established by the reported single-GPU setup.

Reproducibility—important experimental details are missing: the exact trace segment and sampling seed, LongBench subsets and length handling, offline backlog construction, batch/chunk limits, profiler configuration, and the full adaptive checkpointing policy. No code artifact is identified. Repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, and the aggregation windows underlying time-varying P99 plots are also unspecified. These omissions matter because tail latency and burst handling are the principal outcomes.

Presentation and positioning need correction beyond cosmetic editing. Figures 5–7 label the system 'Concerto' rather than ConServe, and Section 6.4.1's reported 446 ms after a 71.4% reduction from 1346 ms is arithmetically inconsistent. Related-work claims that existing systems assume constant arrivals or cannot support both workload classes are overly categorical. A clearer account of what is newly established relative to existing preemption, chunked-prefill, and asynchronous-offloading mechanisms would strengthen the originality claim.

strengths: Significance: Harvesting spare capacity for offline inference while protecting interactive latency is a useful systems problem. The manuscript clearly motivates why priority scheduling alone can fail through compute blocking and KV-cache swapping.

Originality: The contribution is a coherent LLM-specific integration of layer-level preemption, incremental KV-cache checkpointing, background prefetching, and SLO-aware batching. Exploiting immutable KV states to reduce the cost of subsequent preemption is a particularly useful design insight.

Soundness: The implemented prototype and experiments provide encouraging evidence. Evaluation includes a real arrival trace, synthetic ON/OFF transitions, burstiness and request-rate sweeps, and component ablations. Figure 8 supports the qualitative conclusion that checkpointing and prefetching recover throughput sacrificed by latency-aware scheduling.

Presentation: The architectural overview and Figure 4 explain the mechanisms and their interactions well. Implementation details include the vLLM version, CUDA streams, cache mappings, and preemption instrumentation. No material research-ethics concern is evident from the described work.
weaknesses: Soundness—central quantitative claims are inconsistent. Section 6.2 reports 3702 versus 1999 tokens/s, which yields approximately 1.85× throughput, not the 2.35× repeated in the abstract and conclusion of that experiment. Figure 5 calls 86% an offline-throughput ratio, although 3702/4308 compares the reported overall throughputs. Section 6.4.1 also gives a vLLM++ TTFT of 1346 ms under conditions described as matching Figure 7, whereas Section 6.3.2 reports a minimum of 4980 ms. These discrepancies require reconciliation before the headline gains can be trusted.

Soundness and reproducibility—the scheduling pseudocode contradicts the intended behavior. Algorithm 2, lines 10–11, exits when predicted latency exceeds the TTFT objective, precisely when preemption should be considered; its break also appears outside a loop. Algorithm 1 defines τ as remaining capacity but subtracts request tokens when removing a request in line 31. These could be transcription errors rather than implementation failures, but the manuscript does not provide a consistent executable specification of its central scheduler.

Evaluation—the baselines do not establish the claimed advantage over strong alternative co-serving policies. Online-Only receives no offline work, while the authors' vLLM++ deliberately batches aggressively without an SLO constraint. Although enabling chunked prefill is a positive fairness measure, an independently tuned priority baseline with conservative token budgets is needed to separate benefits of the proposed mechanisms from avoiding an unsuitable batching configuration. The 84× reduction should be qualified as a comparison against this particular baseline.

Soundness—the language of performance isolation is stronger than the evidence. Figure 7 shows TTFT rising substantially with load and burstiness, and Figure 5 appears to include a ConServe TTFT excursion above the SLO despite claims of consistently remaining below it. Maintaining latency close to Online-Only is distinct from guaranteeing SLO attainment. The paper should report violation fractions, percentile aggregation windows, profiler prediction errors, and the operating conditions under which its isolation claims hold.

Scope and limitations—all reported evaluation uses Llama-2-7B on one A100-40GB GPU. This supports a specialized contribution, but does not substantiate the discussion's broader claims about tensor/pipeline parallelism, long contexts, multiple models, or compatibility with disaggregation. In particular, distributed synchronization is central to the preemption design but is not evaluated across GPUs. The measured scope should be distinguished clearly from proposed extensions.

Reproducibility—important details remain unspecified: exact trace sampling parameters and seeds, LongBench subsets and length handling, offline backlog construction, baseline batching and memory settings, profiler interpolation, and the adaptive checkpoint-rate rule. No code artifact is identified, and repeated-run uncertainty is not reported. The asynchronous implementation also needs to explain how checkpoint completion is established before source blocks are reclaimed or prefetched blocks are consumed; absence of dependencies with the current computation alone does not establish safe reuse.

strengths: Significance: Harvesting spare capacity for offline inference using the same loaded model addresses a useful deployment problem. The reported improvements are substantial: Table 2 shows 1553 versus 895 offline tokens/s for ConServe and Sarathi-P on the mixed workload, while reducing P99 TTFT from 2.91 to 1.14 seconds.

Originality: The coordinated design of context-aware scheduling, layer-wise preemption, and incremental KV checkpointing is a meaningful systems contribution. Its value lies in making these mechanisms work together for autoregressive inference.

Soundness: Evaluation covers three model sizes, tensor parallelism, real traces, and sensitivity to arrival variability and sequence lengths. Section 6.5 provides useful component evidence: scheduling reduces P99 TBT from 375 to 73 ms, preemption further reduces TTFT, and checkpointing improves offline throughput by 1.29×.

Presentation and reproducibility: The motivation and architecture are clearly explained, particularly the state-management alternatives in Figure 5. The paper specifies hardware, precision, software versions, and several implementation details.
weaknesses: Soundness—central latency model: Section 4.2 predicts batch latency using only aggregate compute tokens P and context tokens C, with attention cost proportional to P(P+C). For independent requests, attention work instead depends on per-request token/context combinations; batches with identical aggregate P and C can have substantially different attention costs. The claimed prediction error below 4% lacks a defined error statistic, profiling grid, held-out evaluation, or tail-error analysis. Consequently, the model's reliability on heterogeneous mixed batches—the basis of safe admission—is not established.

Soundness—SLO claims exceed the evidence: The paper repeatedly claims strict guarantees, but supplies a predictive heuristic without conservative error margins, admission control, or explicit feasible-load assumptions. Algorithm 1 does not explicitly account for preemption overhead or existing requests' deadline slack. Section 6.2 reports attainment as low as 86% when targeting Online-Only's P99 latency, and average TTFT/TBT increases of 25%/19%. These results support a useful empirical tradeoff, rather than the stated guarantees.

Evaluation fairness: DistServe-P uses separate prefill and decode GPU sets, yet Figures 6 and 8 label configurations as one H100, and the 70B setup specifies four GPUs already needed for one model replica. The actual allocation, sharing arrangement, and resource normalization for DistServe-P are unexplained. Moreover, Figure 6(b) keeps baseline throughput constant across SLO targets instead of showing their tuned latency-throughput frontiers. These omissions materially weaken comparisons against the strongest alternatives.

Implementation correctness and limitations: Section 5 states that checkpoint/prefetch streams require no synchronization, but producing cache entries, finishing their copies before eviction or reuse, and consuming prefetched entries require ordering. The manuscript does not explain these dependencies or validate output equivalence under repeated mid-iteration preemption. Section 4.4 also claims host memory is strictly bounded by GPU memory, which does not follow when multiple evicted requests retain checkpoints while new requests occupy the GPU; an explicit bound or eviction policy is needed.

Reproducibility and statistical support: No code artifact is identified, and key details are missing: baseline chunk sizes and tuning ranges, fitted profiler parameters, trace segment and scaling, synthetic run durations, repetitions, and uncertainty estimates. P99 TTFT plotted in five-second windows needs accompanying request counts to establish statistical meaning. These gaps are particularly consequential for tail-latency claims.

Scope, presentation, and ethics: Online-Only and Non-Preemptive are useful references, but their designation as optimal bounds is not established. Limitations should explicitly cover same-model workloads, host-memory pressure, and offline starvation under sustained online demand. No material ethical violation is apparent, although treatment of the university-derived trace's privacy and permitted use is not discussed. Overall, the contribution is promising, but unresolved soundness and comparison issues prevent acceptance.

strengths: Significance: Co-serving latency-sensitive online inference and best-effort offline inference is a useful problem. Sharing model weights while harvesting spare capacity could improve serving efficiency without requiring separate training workloads.

Originality: The combination of context-aware token budgeting, layer-wise preemption, and incremental KV checkpointing is a substantive systems contribution. Its value lies in coordinating these mechanisms for autoregressive inference, even though preemption and background checkpointing have established precedents.

Empirical merits: The evaluation covers three model sizes, tensor parallelism, real workload traces, and sensitivity to arrival burstiness and sequence length. The ablations in §6.5 provide useful evidence: scheduling reduces P99 TBT from 375 ms to 73 ms, layer-wise preemption further reduces TTFT, and incremental cache management improves offline throughput by 1.29×.

Presentation and transparency: The motivation and component-level organization are clear, particularly the cache-management illustration in Figure 5. Hardware, precision, engine version, and several runtime settings are disclosed. §6.4 also usefully identifies workload regimes where gains diminish. No material research-ethics concern is evident from the described work.
weaknesses: Soundness—latency predictor: The central model in §4.2 uses aggregate compute tokens P and context tokens C, with attention cost proportional to P(P+C). For independent requests, attention work instead depends on per-request quantities, approximately the sum of p_i(p_i+c_i); identical aggregate P and C can therefore represent substantially different workloads. The manuscript does not explain how this loss of information is handled. The claimed prediction error below 4% lacks a held-out evaluation, error distribution, and breakdown across mixed prefill/decode batches. This matters because the scheduler relies on prediction accuracy to protect latency.

Soundness—SLO claims exceed the evidence: Algorithm 1 compares predicted remaining execution plus incoming work against a TTFT objective, but does not explicitly account for accumulated waiting time of queued requests, preemption overhead, or prediction uncertainty. No admission-control or feasible-load condition establishes when the objective can be met. Empirically, §6.2 reports attainment as low as 86% at an SLO defined by Online-Only's P99 latency. These results demonstrate useful latency control with sufficient slack, rather than the repeatedly claimed strict guarantees.

Evaluation—baseline comparability is insufficiently established: §6.1 describes DistServe-P as using separate GPU sets and tuning prefill/decode ratios, while Figure 6 labels the smaller-model experiments as running on one H100. The actual allocation, colocation arrangement, and resource normalization are not explained. All baselines are author ports or extensions, without validation against their original implementations. Moreover, Figure 6(b) leaves baseline throughput fixed while ConServe adapts to the SLO; a per-SLO chunk-size sweep would provide a stronger throughput–latency comparison. The extreme DistServe-P degradation in Table 2 makes these details especially consequential.

Soundness—cache correctness and resource bounds need clarification: §5 asserts that checkpointing/prefetching and computation require no cross-stream synchronization, but does not specify how newly written cache entries become safe to copy, when prefetched entries become readable, or how pages are protected from reuse during transfers. No output-equivalence validation under repeated preemption is reported. The claim in §4.4 that host-memory footprint is strictly bounded by GPU memory also needs an explicit policy: retaining checkpoints for evicted requests while admitting new ones can exceed that bound. These are unresolved implementation questions, not demonstrated failures.

Reproducibility and statistical evidence: The manuscript supplies no artifact link, fitted coefficients, profiling grid, precise baseline tuning configurations, repeated-run uncertainty, or clearly specified synthetic experiment durations. Real-trace evaluation uses one selected 10-minute segment, and P99 TTFT is plotted in five-second windows without reporting the number of requests per window. These omissions limit independent reproduction and confidence in tail-latency robustness.

Presentation and scope: Calling Online-Only 'latency optimal' and Non-Preemptive 'throughput optimal' overstates what these reference configurations establish; neither is a proven bound. Figure 2 also defines GPU utilization as offered load divided by maximum achievable load, which does not directly measure hardware utilization. The acknowledged workload limitations are helpful, but deployment assumptions such as same-model co-serving, abundant host memory, and behavior under sustained online saturation need clearer treatment. Overall, the useful prototype and promising measurements do not yet resolve the central prediction, comparison, and correctness questions sufficiently for acceptance.

strengths: Significance: Co-serving latency-sensitive online requests and best-effort offline inference using the same model is a useful systems problem. Sharing model weights and harvesting spare capacity could materially improve deployment efficiency.

Originality: The contribution is a coherent integration of context-aware token scheduling, sub-iteration preemption, and incremental KV checkpointing. The underlying ideas have precedents, but their coordinated application to autoregressive co-serving provides a meaningful systems contribution.

Empirical merits: Experiments cover three model sizes, tensor parallelism, realistic long-context offline workloads, and sensitivity to arrival rates, burstiness, and sequence lengths. Table 2 reports substantial improvements over Sarathi-P; on the mixed workload, offline throughput increases from 895 to 1553 tokens/s while P99 TTFT falls from 2.91 to 1.14 seconds.

Presentation and implementation: The motivation and three-component design are clearly organized. Section 6.5 provides useful incremental ablations and measured overheads, including 13 ms preemption responsiveness and approximately 1.1% execution overhead in the reported configuration.
weaknesses: Soundness of the latency model: Section 4.2 models batch attention using P(P+C), with P and C described as aggregate token counts. Attention actually depends on how tokens and contexts are distributed across independent requests; batches with identical totals can have different attention costs. The claimed prediction error below 4% lacks a held-out evaluation, error distribution, or characterization of tested batch compositions. Since scheduling relies directly on this predictor, validation on heterogeneous prefill/decode batches and tail underprediction is essential.

SLO claims exceed the evidence: Section 6.2 reports attainment as low as 86% when targeting the online-only P99 latency, despite repeated claims of strict guarantees. Algorithm 1 does not explicitly account for individual queued-request deadlines, prediction uncertainty, or preemption overhead. The results support improved empirical latency isolation under the tested conditions, but the conditions needed for 99% attainment should be specified and tested.

Baseline fairness is insufficiently established: DistServe-P requires separate prefill and decode GPU allocations, yet Figure 6 labels configurations as one H100 or four H100s without specifying its total resource allocation or throughput normalization. Exact tuning configurations are omitted. Moreover, baselines remain fixed across the SLO sweep; retuning chunk budgets for each target would provide a stronger latency-throughput comparison. Online-Only and Non-Preemptive are useful reference policies, but their designation as optimal bounds is not established.

State-management correctness and bounds need clarification: Section 5 asserts that checkpoint and compute streams require no synchronization, without explaining ordering between newly produced KV data, checkpoint completion, and page reuse after preemption. No output-equivalence or preemption stress tests are reported. Section 4.4 also claims host memory is bounded by physical GPU memory, but does not specify a policy enforcing this when checkpointed, evicted requests accumulate.

Reproducibility and statistical evidence are incomplete: Hardware, software versions, and broad workloads are documented, but no code artifact, precise profiler grid, fitted parameters, baseline configurations, trace-window selection, seeds, or repeated-run uncertainty are provided. The real-trace evaluation uses one ten-minute segment, and five-second P99 reporting lacks sample counts. These omissions make the central tail-latency results difficult to independently assess.

Limitations and ethics: The discussion should explicitly bound applicability to same-model workloads, available host-memory bandwidth, and sufficient spare capacity; offline starvation under sustained online load is not evaluated. No material ethical concern is apparent from the described public-dataset experiments. Overall, the engineering merits are substantial, but unresolved predictor validation, comparison fairness, and reproducibility issues warrant revision before acceptance.
